title: U.S. House · New York's 24th District
area: Western and central New York, including Niagara, Orleans, Genesee, Wyoming and Livingston counties, plus parts of Monroe and Ontario counties.

context.text: Alissa Ellman defeated Diana Kastenbaum in the June 23, 2026 Democratic primary, 61.7%-38.1%. The Republican and Conservative primaries were canceled; incumbent Claudia Tenney advanced without appearing on either ballot.

candidates.name: Claudia Tenney
candidates.currentRole: U.S. Representative, NY-24 (since 2023; previously NY-22, 2017-2019 and 2021-2023)

summary.text: Claudia Tenney is the Republican and Conservative incumbent, an attorney, small-business owner and former New York State Assembly member. She was first elected to the House in 2016, lost the seat in 2018, and returned after winning in 2020. She serves on the Ways and Means, Intelligence, and Science, Space, and Technology committees.

background.text: Born in New Hartford, New York, in 1961, the daughter of the late John R. Tenney, a justice of the New York Supreme Court in the Fifth Judicial District from 1969 through 2003.

Earned a bachelor's degree in political science from Colgate University in 1983 and a J.D. from the University of Cincinnati (Taft College of Law) in 1987; her office says she is admitted to the bar in New York, Connecticut and Florida and to all federal courts.
Worked as an attorney, including as a partner at the Utica-area firm Groben, Gilroy, Oster, and Saunders and later in her own private practice in Clinton, New York.

Established Tenney Media Group in 1997 and served as its publisher and corporate counsel; the company published community newspapers founded by her family, a division that was sold to Gannett in 2004.
Co-owned and served as legal counsel to Mid-York Press, Inc., a commercial printing and manufacturing firm in Sherburne started by her grandfather in 1946.
Was first elected to the New York State Assembly on November 2, 2010, and served from 2011 to 2016.

Was first elected to the U.S. House on November 8, 2016, and served on the Financial Services Committee in the 115th Congress; she lost the seat in 2018 to Anthony Brindisi and was elected again in November 2020.

Serves on the House Committee on Ways and Means (Health and Trade subcommittees), the Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence, and the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology (Energy subcommittee) in the 119th Congress.
According to her office, she is the mother of a U.S. Naval Academy graduate who is an active-duty Major in the U.S. Marine Corps.

positions.summary: Her official site says she cosponsored and voted for the SAVE Act, which would require proof of citizenship for federal elections, and urges the Senate to pass it.
positions.quote: As Chair of the Election Integrity Caucus, I cosponsored and voted in support of the SAVE Act. This critical bill will safeguard the integrity of each citizen’s vote by amending the National Voter Registration Act of 1993 to require proof of citizenship for federal elections.

positions.summary: Her official site says she has opposed War Powers Resolutions seeking to end President Trump's military operations against Iran and stands behind those operations.
positions.quote: That is why I have consistently opposed War Powers Resolutions to prematurely end President Trump’s efforts to prevent a nuclear Iran.

positions.summary: Her official site endorses Executive Order 14201 restricting transgender athletes' participation in women's sports, and says she cosponsored the Protection of Women and Girls in Sports Act.
positions.quote: Fortunately, President Trump issued Executive Order 14201 entitled “Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports” to enforce women’s Title IX protections and preserve fair athletic opportunities for women and girls.

positions.summary: Her official site says she has called for Albany to reverse New York's 2019 climate law (CLCPA), calling its mandates unrealistic and its effects disastrous.
positions.quote: This is why I have called for Albany to reverse this disastrous law.

positions.summary: Her official site says she opposed New York's SAFE Act, introduced legislation to repeal it, and will oppose efforts to further restrict gun ownership.
positions.quote: During my time in the New York State Assembly, I opposed the onerous NY SAFE Act and was the first to introduce formal legislation to repeal this law that infringed on the rights of all law-abiding gun owners.

positions.summary: Her official site criticizes New York's ban on local 287(g) agreements with ICE, says cooperation with federal immigration authorities is essential, and describes the Secure America Act's roughly $70 billion for CBP and ICE as giving officers the resources to enforce immigration laws.
positions.quote: The Secure America Act gave our frontline law enforcement officers the resources they need to keep our borders secure, stop the flow of fentanyl into our communities, and enforce our nation's immigration laws.

record.text: Serves on the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology (Energy subcommittee), the House Committee on Ways and Means (Health and Trade subcommittees), and the Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence (Defense Intelligence and Overhead Architecture; National Intelligence Enterprise subcommittees) in the 119th Congress.

summary.text: Alissa Ellman is a veteran and former special education teacher and Department of Veterans Affairs employee who lives in Lockport. She won the June 2026 Democratic primary and is also the Working Families Party nominee. She says she entered the race after her VA job was cut in 2025 federal staffing reductions, and she is running on affordability, healthcare, public education and rural infrastructure.

background.text: Grew up in Houghton, New York, a rural hamlet of fewer than 2,000 people; news reports describe her as an Allegany County native.
Served in the U.S. Army National Guard from 2001 to 2007 and describes herself as a disabled combat veteran; news reports say she served at Bagram Air Base in Afghanistan.
Describes herself as a cancer survivor after toxic exposure in Afghanistan; WRVO reported she was diagnosed with pheochromocytoma, a rare adrenal cancer.
Earned a bachelor's degree from Niagara University in 2013.
Worked as a special education teacher before becoming an employee of the Department of Veterans Affairs, according to news reports and her Ballotpedia survey.

Says her VA job (in Buffalo) was eliminated in the first round of federal staffing cuts in 2025; WRVO reported she attended President Trump's March 2025 address to Congress as a guest of Sen. Chuck Schumer.
Announced her candidacy in July 2025 and won the June 23, 2026 Democratic primary over Diana Kastenbaum.

priorities.text: Cost of living, including expanding access to affordable childcare, supporting small businesses and expanding the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit.
Rural infrastructure, including funding to expand bus networks and modernize water systems in rural communities.
Organized labor, including passing the PRO Act and ending right-to-work laws.

positions.summary: Her campaign site says she has long supported reproductive freedom.
positions.quote: Alissa has long supported LGBTQ+ rights, reproductive freedom, and equal rights for all Americans.

positions.summary: Told the Niagara Gazette she wants an expansion of Medicare.
positions.quote: I want an expansion of Medicare.

statements.quote: Expanding access to affordable childcare so parents don’t have to choose between earning a living and caring for their children.

researchNotes: Removed an unverified claim about Tenney's vote on the Respect for Marriage Act sourced only to her opponent's campaign site, since it could not be confirmed against an official roll call within this session; her voting record on that and other bills is covered separately by the script that adds federal key votes. Tenney has not completed Ballotpedia's 2026 Candidate Connection survey and her current campaign-site issues page was not accessible, limiting her priorities/positions to committee assignments and dated past statements. Pass 2 (Oct. 2026): added a healthcare position from Niagara Gazette coverage and a child-care statement from her priorities page; her site's priorities page is third-person, and no direct quotes were found on guns, tariffs or taxes on high earners. Biography for Ellman combines her Ballotpedia Candidate Connection survey with local news coverage because her campaign site has no biography page that could be loaded; Tenney's official bio gives no year of birth, so the Ballotpedia year is used.
